title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation
authors: Ye Feng
abstract: This paper formulates a kinematically and variationally consistent phase-field theory for cohesive fracture at finite deformation. The theory introduces an independent compliance-damage field, which accommodates both diffuse distributions and singular concentrations. The phase-field is thereby freed from the dual burden of describing crack geometry and material degradation. A rank-one additive split of the deformation gradient makes separation explicit through independent crack-strain and reference-normal fields. All fields are governed by a single principle of minimum potential energy, which consistently couples nonlinear bulk deformation, crack separation, and crack-plane rotation. One-dimensional energy comparisons show that minimization favors Dirac-type concentration of compliance damage and crack strain. Strong displacement discontinuities thus emerge naturally at a finite phase-field length without being prescribed a priori, while the phase-field remains continuous. The concentrated energy recovers the exact bulk--interface structure of a sharp-crack cohesive zone model. General objective hyperelastic bulk potentials and admissible mixed-mode cohesive laws can therefore be prescribed independently, with the nominal traction--separation law unaffected by the bulk law or phase-field length. Diffuse damage can coexist with concentrated cracks, retaining deformation modes for bulk-energy relaxation during nucleation. Two- and three-dimensional examples validate the theory across large stretches, finite rotations, and complex crack paths. Notably, the computed near-tip Cauchy stress closely matches the analytical 1/r crack-tip asymptotic solution of Long et al. (2011) outside the cohesive zone.

infographic.key_insight: An independent compliance-damage field lets sharp cohesive cracks emerge at finite phase-field length while keeping the phase-field continuous.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports large-deformation fracture modeling with independently prescribed bulk material behavior and mixed-mode traction–separation laws.
method: Separate crack geometry from material degradation using an independent compliance-damage field.
Use a rank-one additive deformation-gradient split to represent crack separation and orientation.
Couple bulk deformation, crack opening, and crack-plane rotation through minimum potential energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: One-dimensional energy comparisons favor concentrated cracks, while 2D and 3D examples demonstrate finite-deformation behavior and near-tip stresses closely matching the analytical 1/r asymptote outside the cohesive zone.
infographic.watch_item: Numerical implementation must resolve concentrated compliance damage and crack strain; the abstract does not establish mesh sensitivity or computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation

title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
authors: Luyao Zhu, Fangfang Zhang, Yi Mei, Ke Chen, Mengjie Zhang
abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

infographic.key_insight: Surrogate-assisted genetic programming learns scheduling rules across changing tasks while reducing catastrophic forgetting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets adaptive production scheduling in dynamic flexible job shops, rather than solid mechanics or constitutive modeling.
method: Adaptive two-stage training balances learning new tasks with retaining prior knowledge.
Task-similarity weighting regulates knowledge reuse across sequential scheduling tasks.
A distance-constrained surrogate model improves fitness estimation accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on sequential heterogeneous scheduling tasks with job or batch arrivals report reduced forgetting and stronger adaptability than several comparison methods.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative gains or computational costs, limiting assessment of practical deployment benefits.
infographic.paper_title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling

title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate
authors: Patrick Kurzeja, Felix Rörentrop, Kai Langenfeld, Jörn Mosler
abstract: Fracture in food can be undesired during production and transportation but also intended during cutting, grinding or mastication. The associated peak load, the deformation at failure and the resulting fragment geometry are all product properties. This work condenses the modeling of such fracture into a physically rigorous recipe that considers the practical constraints imposed by finite element simulations where necessary and applies idealized theoretical assessments where applicable. Cooled dark chocolate serves as a reproducible model material. Two well-established modeling frameworks for Griffith-type brittle fracture are assessed at an affordable spatial discretization: a sharp-interface and a diffuse phase-field approach. The assessment covers the choice of numerical framework, its discretization and a staged identification of the model parameters. Each parameter is identified from the loading stage that governs it: elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force, and the phase-field width last. The phase-field width interferes with the structural response, crack curvature and stress fields, depending on its lower bound set by the affordable spatial resolution. Elastic slope, peak force and crack path therefore cannot be met practically by a single parameter set. The objective must be fixed for the calibration of the model parameters and reported together with the numerical parameters and the boundary value problem.

infographic.key_insight: At affordable mesh resolution, one parameter set cannot simultaneously match elastic slope, peak force and crack path, so fracture calibration must prioritize a stated objective.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physically consistent fracture calibration can support simulations of brittle-food breakage during production, transport, cutting and mastication.
method: Compare sharp-interface and diffuse phase-field models of Griffith-type brittle fracture in cooled dark chocolate.
Identify elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, then critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force.
Calibrate phase-field width last and report the objective, numerical parameters and boundary value problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: The case study assesses both frameworks at affordable spatial discretization and finds that phase-field width affects structural response, crack curvature and stress fields.
infographic.watch_item: Affordable mesh resolution imposes a lower bound on phase-field width, limiting simultaneous agreement across response metrics.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate

title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization
authors: Siva Viknesh, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: High-Péclet-number transport problems give rise to thin boundary layers with steep near-wall gradients whose accurate solution requires high-resolution meshes and could challenge inverse modeling. To address this challenge, we develop an overlapping Schwarz domain-decomposition framework grounded in perturbation theory, in which an inner equation governs near-wall dynamics and an outer equation governs bulk transport, and both subproblems are discretized using the finite element method and assembled into a fully differentiable multidomain physics solver. The formulation permits coarser mesh resolutions, reducing computational cost relative to a single-domain formulation. Exploiting the differentiability of the coupled solver, we formulate inverse problems in which the governing equations and boundary conditions are imposed as hard constraints, with the Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity. To accelerate the resulting adjoint-based optimization, we integrate large language models (LLMs) into the inverse workflow in two distinct configurations: a standalone optimizer that proposes successive parameter updates from the adjoint-computed sensitivities and an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) approach with access to the complete solver workflow, enabling it to perform multistage optimization procedures. The agentic AI configuration is shown to be most advantageous when the spatially varying unknown is represented in a functional basis rather than a high-dimensional nodal field representation. In this case, the AI agent grows the library of candidate basis functions during optimization under a prescribed admission policy, admitting predefined families in stages and initializing their parameters. In short, our proposed framework integrates Schwarz-coupled differentiable physics with agentic AI optimization for the inverse modeling of multiscale transport problems.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable Schwarz-coupled finite element solver combines near-wall and bulk transport models, enabling inverse modeling of thin boundary layers with agentic AI optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets high-Péclet transport problems where steep near-wall gradients make conventional single-domain simulations and parameter identification computationally demanding.
method: Use perturbation theory to formulate overlapping near-wall and bulk equations, discretized with finite elements.
Enforce governing equations and boundary conditions as hard constraints, with Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity.
Use adjoint sensitivities for LLM-guided updates or an AI agent that stages optimization and expands a prescribed functional basis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports lower computational cost than a single-domain formulation and greater agentic AI benefit for functional-basis unknowns than nodal fields, but provides no numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Agentic optimization benefits may depend on the unknown's representation and the prescribed basis-admission policy.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization

title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
authors: Alexander Safonov
abstract: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.

infographic.key_insight: A two-stage diffusion model reproduces branching ribs followed by pore-forming bridges through a switch in how local flux drives growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links diffusion-driven material deposition to density-based topology optimization, offering a route to simulate evolving porous architectures on a fixed finite element mesh.
method: Represent material with a density field on an active layer of a fixed finite element mesh.
Stage 1: promote dendritic growth where a local diffusive-flux stimulus exceeds a threshold.
Stage 2: invert the stimulus so high local flux suppresses precipitation and stabilizes pores.
infographic.evidence_signal: A reference calculation produces approximately uniformly spaced pores absent near domain edges, qualitatively consistent with diatom valve observations.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative validation against cryo-electron tomography is proposed rather than demonstrated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity

title: $W^{1,p}$ error estimates of an IPDG and a class of HDG methods for the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains
authors: Haitao Leng, Weifeng Qiu
abstract: This paper analyzes a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) method, a hybrid mixed DG method, and two representative hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) methods for the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains. For any fixed $ε\in (0,\frac{1}{2})$, we first derive optimal discrete $W^{1,p}$ error estimates for $2\leq p<\frac{1}ε$ by combining the interface Green's functions developed in \cite{lq2026} with the Fubini-type weighted estimates established in this paper. These error estimates lead to discrete $W^{1,q}$-$W^{1,p}$ inf-sup stability for $2\leq q<\frac{1}ε$, where $q$ is the conjugate number of $p$ such that $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1$. Using this stability result and a suitably constructed dual problem, we extend the optimal error estimates to $\frac{1}{1-ε}<p<2$ and subsequently establish the corresponding inf-sup stability for $\frac{1}{1-ε}< q<2$. Thus, both optimal discrete $W^{1,p}$ error estimates and discrete $W^{1,q}$-$W^{1,p}$ inf-sup stability hold throughout the range $\frac{1}{1-ε}<p<\frac{1}ε$, with $q=p/(p-1)$. Note that all of the aforementioned results are free of logarithmic factors and also hold on polyhedral meshes (except for the hybrid mixed DG method). Compared with the conforming finite element method (FEM), establishing such error estimates and inf-sup stability results for DG methods on convex polyhedral domains is more delicate because their analysis involves mesh-dependent norms. Consequently, the operator interpolation theory employed for conforming FEMs cannot be directly applied to DG methods. Finally, a numerical example is presented to illustrate the theoretical results.

infographic.key_insight: For the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains, the analyzed DG methods achieve optimal discrete W^{1,p} error estimates and conjugate-exponent inf-sup stability without logarithmic factors for 1/(1−ε) < p < 1/ε, with fixed ε ∈ (0, 1/2).
infographic.engineering_relevance: These guarantees support reliable gradient approximation and stability assessment for DG discretizations of elliptic PDEs used in computational engineering.
method: Analyze symmetric IPDG, hybrid mixed DG, and two representative HDG methods.
Combine interface Green’s functions with new Fubini-type weighted estimates.
Use inf-sup stability and a dual problem to extend estimates below p = 2.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical error and stability guarantees, illustrated by one numerical example.
infographic.watch_item: Results assume convex polyhedral domains; the extension to polyhedral meshes excludes the hybrid mixed DG method.
infographic.paper_title: $W^{1,p}$ error estimates of an IPDG and a class of HDG methods for the Poisson problem on convex polyhedral domains

title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning
authors: Dex Doksoo Lee, Jehyeon Shin, Yue Yu, Sunkyu Yu, Junsuk Rho, Wei Chen
abstract: In multiscale systems, nonlocal interactions among spatially distributed constituents can unlock collective, potentially emergent behavior irreducible to individual constituent responses. Beyond characterization, nonlocality in multiscale systems is increasingly viewed as a design element across fracture mechanics, wave physics, and disordered systems. Existing nonlocality theories provide rigorous descriptions and mechanistic insight, but often require prescribed analytic forms, range, symmetries, or periodicity. Machine learning offers a data-driven route to learn interactions, yet principled approaches that tie the network design to physical theory remain nascent. Here we present domain-decomposition attention neural operator (DANO), which learns configuration-dependent interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations from field data alone. Through a case study in large-scale optical metasurfaces, we demonstrate DANO's full-field prediction under geometric heterogeneity and across drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design, with learned interactions validated through physics-based interrogation. As an AI-for-Science tool, it supports interaction discovery and scalable, customizable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, including virtual-reality optics.

infographic.key_insight: DANO learns configuration-dependent nonlocal interactions from field data, enabling full-field prediction and inverse design in heterogeneous metamaterials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Demonstrated on optical metasurfaces, the approach could inform scalable design of nonlocal multiscale systems, though fracture and damage applications remain untested here.
method: Uses a domain-decomposition attention neural operator.
Learns interactions in heterogeneous systems governed by linear field equations.
Interrogates learned interactions using physics-based validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports full-field prediction across geometric heterogeneity and drive conditions, small-to-large domain transfer, and multifunctional inverse design in large-scale optical metasurfaces.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability to nonlinear fracture and damage is not established by the reported linear-field optical case study.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Nonlocal Interactions in Large-Scale Heterogeneous Metamaterials through Scientific Machine Learning

title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass
authors: Ankit Singh, Alessio Zaccone, Oleg Gendelman, Valeriy V. Ginzburg
abstract: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $φ(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.

infographic.key_insight: A nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model connects metallic-glass yielding and flow to relaxation dynamics measured independently in stress-relaxation tests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports prediction of temperature- and strain-rate-dependent elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow in metallic glasses.
method: Combine a nonlinear elastic spring with a stretched-exponential dashpot in a Maxwell-type element.
Determine reference material time X₀(ε) from stress relaxation and nonlinear material time X(ε) from elastic–viscoplastic strain decomposition.
Use the Eyring-type ratio φ(ε) = X(ε)/X₀(ε) to quantify deformation-induced changes in relaxation dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports independent stress-relaxation measurements and stress–strain responses as inputs, but provides no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires separate relaxation measurements; predictive accuracy beyond the studied conditions is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass

title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
authors: Volker Kempe
abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.

infographic.key_insight: Spiking neural networks could complement transformer-based AI through event-driven computation, local learning, and temporal information coding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Neuromorphic AI may support energy-constrained engineering applications, though the abstract establishes no specific solid-mechanics use case.
method: Explain transformer text generation using ChatGPT as an example.
Compare spike-based coding, local learning, and network design with conventional AI.
Review the Neural Engineering Framework and neuromorphic hardware, including Loihi 2.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual and mathematical monograph, citing energy contrasts but reporting no controlled benchmarks or solid-mechanics validation.
infographic.watch_item: Application-level energy savings and accuracy require validation; the brain's cited 20-watt power consumption is not directly comparable to aggregate model energy use.
infographic.paper_title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI

title: $H^2$-based equilibrated residual error estimates
authors: Kexin Ding, Yuwen Li
abstract: We develop a framework for equilibrated residual a posteriori error analysis of finite element methods, based on decomposing vector- and tensor-valued Sobolev spaces into $H^2$ and $H^1$ spaces. To estimate the residual functional acting on $H^2$ component, the method reconstructs symmetric and piecewise polynomial tensors on vertex patches in broken $H(\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div})$ spaces. We apply the proposed framework to conforming finite element discretizations of biharmonic equation, Poisson's equation, and linear elasticity in mixed form. As a result, we obtain several novel equilibrated residual a posteriori error estimates, providing guaranteed error control for energy error of biharmonic equation, $L^2$ norm error of Poisson's equation, and stress error of mixed linear elasticity. They also serve as the first polynomial-degree-robust a posteriori lower bounds of discretization errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the $H^2$-based error estimators.

infographic.key_insight: An H²-based equilibrated residual framework provides guaranteed finite element error control and polynomial-degree-robust a posteriori lower bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliable error assessment for plate bending, Poisson problems, and mixed linear elasticity, including stress-error control.
method: Decompose vector- and tensor-valued Sobolev spaces into H² and H¹ components.
Reconstruct symmetric, piecewise-polynomial tensors on vertex patches in broken H(div div) spaces.
Use equilibrated residuals to estimate biharmonic energy error, Poisson L² error, and mixed-elasticity stress error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate estimator effectiveness, but the abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or computational-cost results.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires specialized local tensor reconstruction; its computational overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: $H^2$-based equilibrated residual error estimates

title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
authors: Elton Donfack-Siewe, Sylvain Dubreuil, Christian Fagiano, Jérôme Morio, Jean-Philippe Navarro
abstract: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

infographic.key_insight: Scale-driven averaging attenuates variability in panel ultimate load, but spatially correlated interface properties remain essential for predicting early damage initiation and location.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Match stochastic model fidelity to the design criterion: spatially uniform variability for global load capacity and correlated random fields for local skin–stringer bond integrity.
method: Extend likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II interface properties using experimental coupon data.
Propagate interface variability from coupons to aerospace panels with simulation-based stochastic finite elements.
Compare industrial B-basis, spatially uniform variability, and spatially correlated random-field strategies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Coupon experiments support stochastic parameter calibration, while panel simulations show uncertainty attenuation in ultimate load and weak-spot-driven early damage.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative accuracy metrics or panel-scale experimental validation, leaving predictive transfer across scales to be verified.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response

title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
authors: Philipp Bordne, André Biedenkapp
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

infographic.key_insight: Preserving neural-network plasticity improves reinforcement learning robustness on harder stochastic tasks, but TD instability dominates in the most challenging settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These findings may inform robust learning-based engineering controllers under sensor and actuator noise, though solid-mechanics applications were not evaluated.
method: Train Soft Actor-Critic agents on three DeepMind Control tasks.
Introduce controlled observation and action noise.
Evaluate plasticity-preserving methods, including resets and layer normalization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three tasks, plasticity-preserving methods improved robustness on the two harder tasks as observation noise increased, while resets plus layer normalization underperformed resets alone at every tested observation-noise level.
infographic.watch_item: Noise effects depend on task difficulty, so plasticity-preserving interventions should not be assumed to resolve severe TD instability.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments

title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors
authors: Ahanaf Hasan Ariq, Abrar Shahid
abstract: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.

infographic.key_insight: Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA) gates model updates by selecting the largest tested interpolation step whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence stays within a declared budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For adaptive engineering models exposing comparable policy distributions, CABA offers an auditable retention check, but solid-mechanics and constitutive-model performance remain untested.
method: Reserve historical anchors from candidate optimization and compare old and candidate policies on frozen representations.
Test update interpolations and accept the largest coefficient meeting the worst-anchor divergence budget.
Extend anchor retention to protected support only under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition proxy study, CABA at ε = 0.05 reduced mean forgetting from 1.01% to 0.00%, while final average accuracy fell from 93.04% to 88.48%.
infographic.watch_item: Passing the anchor check does not by itself certify off-anchor retention or current-task utility; these require additional assumptions and separate evidence.
infographic.paper_title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors

title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods
authors: Szymon Nosewicz, Marcin Maździarz, Paweł Hołobut, Witold Chromiński, Katarzyna Kowalczyk-Gajewska, Grzegorz Jurczak
abstract: The presented work proposes a multiscale framework for the numerical and analytical determination of the elastic constants of the intermetallic nickel aluminide (NiAl) at the microscopic scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations have been employed to evaluate the stiffness tensors of a single NiAl monocrystalline body with cubic Pm$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The atomistic results were transferred to the upper scale as an input to micromechanical models. Here, finite element modeling (FEM) and analytical homogenization methods were used to simulate the elastic behavior of polycrystalline NiAl, with special attention to grain anisotropy and its morphology. The microstructural features of the heterogeneous body were evaluated experimentally using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and subsequently used to generate a 3D polycrystalline geometric model that preserves realistic distributions of grain orientations and grain sizes. The reconstructed NiAl polycrystal was subjected to uniaxial tensile test simulations using FEM to evaluate the effective Young's modulus ($E$) and Poisson's ratio ($ν$). The numerical results were confronted with the experimental values of $E$ and~$ν$. With these model assumptions, a very good agreement between numerical and experimental results was achieved. Finally, the experimental results were compared with classical analytical estimates. Among the analytical approaches, the Hashin-Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation reproduced the experimental Young's modulus with minor deviations.

infographic.key_insight: Linking atomistic NiAl stiffness to EBSD-informed finite element models predicts polycrystalline elastic properties in very good agreement with experiments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports microstructure-aware prediction of NiAl stiffness while accounting for grain orientations, sizes and morphology.
method: Compute single-crystal NiAl stiffness tensors using atomistic calculations.
Build a 3D polycrystal from EBSD-derived grain orientation and size distributions, then simulate uniaxial tension with FEM.
Compare effective elastic properties with experiments and analytical homogenization estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports very good numerical–experimental agreement for Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio; the Hashin–Shtrikman upper bound and self-consistent approximation closely reproduce experimental Young’s modulus.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement depends on the stated model assumptions; the abstract provides no numerical error metrics or validation beyond elastic response.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale evaluation of the elastic response of polycrystalline NiAl using molecular statics, EBSD-based finite element and analytical homogenization methods

title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
authors: Daniel Levine, David van Dijk, Kenneth Kay
abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.

infographic.key_insight: AutoHebb networks combine meta-learned fixed weights with autonomously gated Hebbian plasticity to support zero-shot inference and continual learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AutoHebb suggests an adaptive-learning approach potentially relevant to constitutive modeling, but the abstract reports no solid-mechanics validation.
method: Meta-learn fixed weights that encode strong inductive biases.
Combine external feedback and internal activity into a global neuromodulatory signal.
Use that signal to gate local three-factor Hebbian updates to plastic weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports success on zero-shot tasks, emergent untrained zero-shot and continual-learning abilities, and performance exceeding modern comparison models, without quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Application to constitutive modeling would require testing physical consistency, stability, and generalization across loading histories.
infographic.paper_title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn

title: A Preconditioned Quantum Linear Solver for Periodic Two-Phase Heat Conduction with Mesh-Independent Condition Number
authors: Krishnan Suresh
abstract: We consider here computational homogenization of a periodic two-phase conduction problem. Quantum linear-system algorithms for its finite element discretization are limited by the condition number of the stiffness matrix. This condition number grows quadratically with the number of elements per side. Classically, preconditioning by the homogeneous (single-phase) operator bounds the condition number by the conductivity contrast, for every mesh size. On a quantum computer, however, a preconditioner encoded as a separate factor multiplies the subnormalizations, and the quadratic dependency returns. In this paper, we absorb the closed-form inverse square root of the homogeneous operator into the finite element factors. The preconditioned operator then becomes the product of a norm-preserving gradient operator $\mat{V}$, a diagonal matrix of scaled conductivities, and $\mat{V}^T$. Each factor has norm at most one. The block encoding therefore has subnormalization one, and its condition number is bounded by just the conductivity contrast, for every mesh size and in every dimension. The operator $\mat{V}$ is applied as a quantum Fourier transform, a small rotation at each wavenumber, and an inverse transform. Quantum singular value transformation then block-encodes the inverse of the preconditioned operator. We test the method numerically on three periodic cells with up to $10^6$ unknowns. The results confirm that the condition number does not depend on the mesh, and the energy-norm error of the inverse is below the polynomial tolerance at every mesh. On meshes of $4 \times 4$ and $8 \times 8$ elements, we also build the entire inverse as one Qiskit circuit and simulate it by state vector, with the rotation at each wavenumber built from uniformly controlled rotations. The output state agrees with the finite element solution to within the polynomial tolerance.

infographic.key_insight: Absorbing the homogeneous operator’s inverse square root into finite element factors yields a quantum-encoded conduction operator with unit subnormalization and a condition number bounded by conductivity contrast, independent of mesh size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach removes a mesh-dependent conditioning bottleneck in quantum linear solves for computational homogenization of periodic two-phase heat conduction.
method: Factor the preconditioned operator using a norm-preserving gradient and scaled diagonal conductivities.
Implement the gradient using quantum Fourier transforms and wavenumber-dependent rotations.
Use quantum singular value transformation to encode the preconditioned inverse.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests on three periodic cells with up to 10^6 unknowns confirmed mesh-independent conditioning and inverse errors below polynomial tolerance; full Qiskit state-vector simulations on 4×4 and 8×8 meshes matched finite element solutions within that tolerance.
infographic.watch_item: Full quantum-circuit validation is limited to small simulated meshes; conditioning still depends on conductivity contrast, and practical hardware advantage remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: A Preconditioned Quantum Linear Solver for Periodic Two-Phase Heat Conduction with Mesh-Independent Condition Number

title: Thermal Stability and Structural Relaxation Kinetics of Commercially Pure Titanium
authors: Y. Semerenko, N. Galtsov, D. Hurova, T. Bednarchuk, P. Zinoviev, V. Zoryansky
abstract: This work explores the structural relaxation of cryorolled commercially pure titanium subjected to subsequent annealing.Nanostructured specimens with an average grain size of ~50 nm were produced by plastic deformation via cryogenic rolling at 100 K to a true strain of 1.20, followed by annealing at 425 K, 525 K, 725 K, and 945 K. Microstructural evolution was examined using electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction. Cryogenic rolling was found to induce pronounced grain fragmentation, with coherent scattering regions (CSRs) of 30-50 nm dominating the substructure. X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that annealing drives crystallite growth: a slight increase at 525 K, accelerated coarsening at 725 K, and complete recrystallization at 945 K. The kinetics of grain growth follow the classical Lifshitz-Slyozov-Wagner model, with a growth exponent of ~4, reflecting the role of triple junctions and defect-controlled boundary diffusion. The activation energy, estimated at ~97 kJ/mol, corresponds to typical values for grain boundary diffusion in α-Ti, confirming that cryogenic deformation produces a highly non-equilibrium microstructure whose relaxation is strongly temperature dependent.

infographic.key_insight: Cryorolled commercially pure titanium develops a ~50 nm grain structure that coarsens during annealing and fully recrystallizes at 945 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Temperature-dependent relaxation informs heat-treatment choices for retaining nanostructure or promoting recrystallization in cryorolled titanium.
method: Cryogenic rolling at 100 K to a true strain of 1.20.
Annealing at 425, 525, 725, and 945 K.
Electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction to characterize structural evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: X-ray diffraction showed slight crystallite growth at 525 K, accelerated coarsening at 725 K, and complete recrystallization at 945 K; reported growth kinetics gave an exponent of ~4 and activation energy of ~97 kJ/mol.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify annealing durations or kinetic-fit uncertainties, limiting direct translation into processing schedules.
infographic.paper_title: Thermal Stability and Structural Relaxation Kinetics of Commercially Pure Titanium

title: Higher-Order QMC Galerkin FEM for Singular Perturbation: Reaction-Diffusion with Affine-Parametric Reaction
authors: Fabian Rohner, Christoph Schwab
abstract: We analyze higher-order quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) Galerkin discretizations for a singularly perturbed reaction-diffusion problem with an affine-parametric reaction coefficient. We derive error estimates that are robust with respect to the perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$. To this end, we establish $\varepsilon$-uniform stability and mixed-parametric regularity estimates in an $\varepsilon$-weighted energy norm, with constants independent of the parameter dimension and of $\varepsilon$. These estimates imply robust dimension truncation estimates and dimension-independent higher-order QMC error bounds for linear quantities of interest. Assuming an abstract, $\varepsilon$-robust finite element approximation property, we combine the parametric estimates with the spatial discretization analysis to derive a general fully discrete QMC-FE error estimate with constants independent of both the parameter dimension and $\varepsilon$. We verify this approximation property for a one-dimensional model problem using continuous piecewise affine finite elements on Shishkin meshes. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted robustness and convergence rates.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order QMC–Galerkin finite element error bounds remain robust as the perturbation parameter ε becomes small, with constants independent of parameter dimension.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty quantification for reaction–diffusion models with thin boundary layers without deterioration of error constants as ε decreases.
method: Establish ε-uniform stability and mixed-parametric regularity in a weighted energy norm.
Combine dimension truncation and higher-order QMC integration for linear quantities of interest.
Couple spatial error estimates with QMC analysis; verify robust approximation using 1D Shishkin-mesh FEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate predicted robustness and convergence rates, while robust spatial approximation is verified for a one-dimensional model with continuous piecewise affine elements.
infographic.watch_item: The general fully discrete guarantee assumes ε-robust finite element approximation, explicitly verified here only for a one-dimensional model.
infographic.paper_title: Higher-Order QMC Galerkin FEM for Singular Perturbation: Reaction-Diffusion with Affine-Parametric Reaction

title: A Differentiable, GPU-Accelerated Finite-Element Formulation in JAX for Large-Deformation Shells with Contact: Application to Patient-Specific Aortic Valve Simulation
authors: Mohsen Nakhaei, Alison M. Pouch, Matthew A. Jolley, Wensi Wu
abstract: Patient-specific aortic-valve models can help assess how tissue properties and geometry influence leaflet deformation and coaptation, with potential to inform intervention planning. Large deformations, near-incompressibility, and evolving contact make these simulations computationally demanding and can challenge nonlinear convergence. Differentiable, GPU-accelerated methods offer efficient derivative evaluation and parallel computation, but their matrix-free application to soft-tissue shells with contact remains less established. We developed a forward solver using tatva's energy-based finite-element framework in JAX. The solver combines finite-strain extensible-director shells, hyperelastic constitutive models, and a finite-range repulsive contact energy. Nonlinear equilibrium is solved using a regularized, matrix-free Newton-Krylov method with two-level preconditioning. Automatic differentiation evaluates tangent-vector products without forming or storing the primary tangent matrix, while GPU execution parallelizes element and quadrature-point computations. Constitutive, shell, contact, and self-contact responses were assessed against analytical, semi-analytical, and published benchmarks. At a contact-free plate equilibrium, implicit sensitivities of the converged apex displacement to constitutive parameters, thickness, and pressure agreed with finite differences from independent nonlinear simulations. Simulations of three patient-specific aortic-valve models (two tricuspid and one bicuspid) achieved final relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4. Median GPU runtimes were approximately 15-25 minutes, with 5.3-6.5-fold speedups relative to corresponding CPU runs on the tested hardware. These results provide component-level verification and demonstrate GPU-accelerated forward valve simulation in the tested cases, supporting future gradient-based inverse studies.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable, matrix-free JAX finite-element solver enables GPU-accelerated simulation of large-deformation aortic-valve shells with contact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster patient-specific valve simulations could support studies of how tissue properties and geometry affect leaflet deformation and coaptation.
method: Energy-based finite-strain extensible-director shells with hyperelastic materials and finite-range repulsive contact.
Regularized matrix-free Newton–Krylov equilibrium solver with two-level preconditioning.
Automatic differentiation for tangent-vector products and GPU-parallel element and quadrature computations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Component benchmarks and contact-free sensitivity checks supported verification; three patient-specific valves reached relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4, with median GPU runtimes of approximately 15–25 minutes and 5.3–6.5× speedups over corresponding CPU runs.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity validation was limited to a contact-free plate, so gradient accuracy for valve simulations with evolving contact remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A Differentiable, GPU-Accelerated Finite-Element Formulation in JAX for Large-Deformation Shells with Contact: Application to Patient-Specific Aortic Valve Simulation

title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations
authors: Timna Böttcher, Rick Ridder, Jan Bender
abstract: We present a new MPM-based solver for perfectly elastic solids, which can recover from strong deformations and naturally allows contact handling. Typical MPM solvers suffer from numerical fracture, where objects break apart even when no plasticity is included in the elasticity model. Previous approaches for perfectly elastic solids solve this by computing forces on a fixed grid in the reference configuration. However, this makes them incompatible with standard collision handling methods. We instead propose a method for deformable solid simulation without numerical fracture, that still computes elastic forces on the current grid. Our method can easily include grid-based collision handling, as commonly used in MPM frameworks. Additionally, we compute the deformation directly from the particle positions and a fixed reference grid, without any updates based on velocity gradients. This facilitates the inclusion of particle-level collision handling and zero-energy mode suppression, which counteracts artifacts from non-linear deformations. As a result, we can efficiently simulate complex scenarios of elastic objects undergoing large deformations, including contact.

infographic.key_insight: Computing total deformation from particle positions and a fixed reference grid enables fracture-free, perfectly elastic MPM while retaining force evaluation on the current grid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports large-deformation elastic solid simulation with contact handling compatible with standard MPM frameworks.
method: Compute deformation directly from particle positions and a fixed reference grid, rather than updating it through velocity gradients.
Evaluate elastic forces on the current grid to support grid-based collision handling.
Accommodate particle-level collisions and suppress zero-energy modes associated with nonlinear deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports complex elastic-object simulations with large deformations and contact, but provides no quantitative accuracy or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness and computational cost of zero-energy mode suppression under extreme deformation require assessment beyond the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations
